article_title: For asylum seekers, at what point do they actually ‘arrive’ in the U.S.?
article_content:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday considered a key question about asylum seekers who arrive at the border: If a prospective migrant presents himself on the Mexican side of it, has he technically arrived in the U.S.?
At the center of arguments before the court was the so-called metering policy, in which border officials can block migrants from stepping foot on U.S. soil where they would be entitled to claim asylum and receive protection from persecution when border crossings reached capacity.
The policy began at the end of the Obama administration, but was championed by President Donald Trump during his first term. Then-President Joe Biden then rescinded the policy when he took office in 2021.
During arguments, the Trump administration indicated it would like to reinstate this policy in the future but would not indicate when or how. “I can’t predict when the next border surge occurs,” said Vivek Suri, assistant to the solicitor general. “But I can say that when it does occur, this is a tool that DHS would want in its toolbox.”
The case — Noem v. Al Otro Lado — came to the Supreme Court after a federal judge in California declared the policy unlawful. In that lower court case, immigrants rights advocates and individual asylum seekers from Central American countries had sued the government, claiming “metering” violated federal immigration law.
Federal law states the government must provide protection for individual migrants who present themselves at a border crossing and fear persecution on the basis of race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership to a particular social group. The law covers any migrant “who is physically present in the United States or who arrives in the United States.”
But just what constitutes “arrival” was a central point of discussion among the justices.
Al Otro Lado argues that immigrants arrive when they present themselves to border officials at a point of entry. The group says the language in the statute implies Congress intended for it “to apply not only to those who have arrived, but to those who are attempting to step over the border.”
The federal government disagrees.
“In ordinary English,” U.S. Solicitor General John D. Sauer writes, “a person ‘arrives in’ a country only when he comes within its borders. A person does not ‘arrive in the United States’ if he is stopped in Mexico.”
Justice Amy Coney Barrett questioned Al Otro Lado’s counsel, asking, “How do you know under your theory when the person is close enough that we could say they have arrived in or arrived in the destination?”
“If it’s not crossing the physical border,” she continued, “what is the magic thing or dispositive thing that we’re looking for where we say, ‘ah, now that person arrives in the United States?’”
